title: Shutdown and equipment care
audience: Trainee or new worker on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Follow manufacturer shut-down/depressurisation, inspect hoses and connections and quarantine defective equipment.
referencesAtStart: Official sources used in this lesson: Safe Work Australia, Working at heights (no date shown); SafeWork NSW, Work safely at heights in construction (no date shown); SafeWork NSW, High risk work licences (last updated 15 June 2026); WorkSafe Victoria, High risk work licence (reviewed 30 June 2026); SafeWork SA, Lowering the height threshold will raise safety standards (news) (05 June 2026); WorkSafe Queensland, Boom-type elevating work platform (no date shown); WorkSafe WA, Boom-type elevating work platform high risk work licence class (published 11 August 2026; last updated 13 August 2026); WorkSafe Tasmania, Check the classes (high risk licensing) (last updated 1 December 2023); Access Canberra, High risk work licences (only a fee period shown, 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026; no publication date); NT WorkSafe, Elevating work platform operation licence requirements (bulletin) (no date shown); South Australian Government, High risk work licence (last updated 10 January 2024); Safe Work Australia, Code of Practice: Elevating work platforms (model code) (December 2025); Safe Work Australia, Guide for managing high pressure water jetting (December 2013; no edition number); NSW Government, Electrical licences and certificates (building and trades) (last updated 23 June 2026).

instruction.heading: Pressure cleaning at height and the access context
instruction.body: This lesson sits in the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, which covers ground-level pressure work and work that is elevated or on a roof. High-pressure water, hoses and lances, the machine's power source, electrical supply, exhaust gas and falls from height are all hazards on this track. Safe Work Australia treats construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres as high risk construction work, and it lists the control order to follow, starting with doing the work from the ground or a solid surface. NSW requires a safe work method statement where a fall could exceed 2 metres. In South Australia, construction work with a risk of falling more than two metres is high-risk from 1 July 2026, and a SWMS is required, according to SafeWork SA's guidance (March 2026, no day shown); the regulation text itself was not read in this pass. The Victorian, Queensland, Western Australian and Tasmanian pages checked do not state a metre threshold for this work. Where the work is above ground level, the employer's written authorisation is needed in addition to any licence the state or territory requires. The authorisation rule is working practice in this course rather than a checked legal rule. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on a roof or on a solar system.

instruction.heading: Why shutdown is still a hazard step
instruction.body: A pressure cleaner can hold energy after the engine or motor has stopped, in the pump, the hose and the lance. The end of a job is therefore a hazard step, not a tidy-up step. The Safe Work Australia guide on high pressure water jetting expects a system to be depressurised and locked off when nobody is attending it, when it is idle, and when parts are being swapped or fixed. The same guide asks that planning and pre-start checks cover isolation steps that use locks and tags. The guide does not give a bleed-down method for each machine, and it does not set a specific stored-energy warning. The manufacturer's full shutdown sequence therefore decides the actual steps for the machine in front of you. Treat every machine as still charged until the checks in this lesson show that it is not. The guide defines high pressure by output rather than by one pressure figure, and it notes that systems below its output definition can still be covered where injury is a foreseeable risk. A small domestic-style machine is therefore not outside the thinking in this lesson.

instruction.heading: Shutdown sequence and pressure release
instruction.body: Use the sequence in the manufacturer's manual for the specific machine. The order matters. Stop the engine or motor and isolate the power or fuel supply the way the manual says. Shut off the water supply to the machine. Release the stored pressure by the method the manufacturer gives, which is commonly done by operating the trigger gun or lance with the supply shut off. Then confirm the machine is safe by checking that the pressure gauge reads nil, if the machine has one, and that no water flows from the lance or nozzle. Only when those checks pass should any hose, lance or fitting be disconnected. Do not open a coupling while the machine still holds pressure, and do not rely on the machine being switched off to mean it is safe. If the machine will not depressurise, or the release method is unclear, stop and call the supervisor. Do not try to force the coupling or strike it.

instruction.heading: Hoses, connections and inspection
instruction.body: Inspect each hose assembly, fitting, coupling, trigger gun, lance and nozzle at the end of every job, and before the first use of the day. The Safe Work Australia guide wants a competent person to look over each hose assembly before every use. It classes a hose with broken wires, a deep abrasion, a kink, a blister or a bubble as defective, and it classes a fitting with a crack, corrosion or damaged threads as defective. Check each connection for leaks at the seal and for wear at the thread. Keep hoses flat, in a place that is cool and not damp, because the guide links hose life to pressure cycling, heat, chemicals and abrasion. The guide does not set a replacement interval, so the manufacturer's data and the business's maintenance schedule must set it. The guide is dated December 2013, so check whether a later edition or the manufacturer's data gives different requirements before relying on it for a particular machine.

instruction.heading: Quarantine and defect reporting
instruction.body: A defective item must be taken out of use at once. Stop using it, tag it as defective, and move it away from the working equipment so that it cannot be picked up by mistake. The guide expects a defective hose to come out of service with a clear marking and tag. It also calls for testing after a hose is new, damaged, re-ended or repaired, keeps test records, and allows only passing hoses back into use. As a trainee, you do not repair the item or test it yourself. Record what you found on the defect log: the item, its identifier if it has one, the date, the defect, and who found it. Report it to the supervisor and request maintenance through the business's own route. Do not fit a spare fitting from another machine, cut out a damaged section and rejoin the hose, or wrap a damaged hose with tape to keep it in service. Each of those actions changes the equipment without authority and removes the record of the defect.

instruction.heading: Chemicals, containers and wash water at shutdown
instruction.body: Chemicals used in pressure cleaning should stay in their original labelled containers, or in containers labelled with the product name and the hazard information that the safety data sheet gives. Keep containers closed when they are not in use and store them as the safety data sheet directs. Do not mix products unless the label or the safety data sheet allows it. Check the safety data sheet for each product before use, and keep the sheets where the team can find them. Until those rules are confirmed for the work site, follow the site rules and the supervisor's instructions, and record how waste and wash water were handled on the job record.

instruction.heading: Competency boundary and the electrical notice
instruction.body: Apply the site-specific risk assessment, the verified local requirements and the equipment manufacturer's instructions. This lesson alone does not grant authorisation for regulated high-pressure jetting, hazardous remediation, electrical isolation, fuel system repair or confined-space work. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work covers the physical work of putting in, fixing, changing, removing or extending an installation, and the licensing page leaves out electrical articles connected to an outlet. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

procedure: Confirm the cleaning area is secured, with the exclusion zone marked and the supervisor informed that shutdown has started.
Stop the engine or motor and isolate the power or fuel supply as the manufacturer's manual directs.
Shut off the water supply to the machine.
Release the stored pressure using the manufacturer's method, with the supply shut off.
Confirm the safe state: the gauge reads nil where fitted, and no water flows from the lance or nozzle.
Disconnect hoses and lances only after the safe-state check passes, and point the lance to a safe direction while doing so.
Collect hoses by coiling them, without dragging them across delicate or sharp surfaces.
Inspect each hose, fitting, coupling, trigger gun, lance and nozzle for defects, leaks and worn threads.
Tag any defective item as defective, move it away from the working equipment and log it.
Return chemicals to their labelled containers, close them and store them as the safety data sheet directs.
Record the defects and maintenance requests on the job record, and report them to the supervisor.
Sign the shutdown checklist once every step is complete and the equipment is recorded as safe or quarantined.

workedExamples.situation: After shutdown, a worker starts to unscrew a hose coupling, and the machine still holds pressure in the hose.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop before the coupling is touched. Confirm the machine is off and the water supply and power or fuel are isolated. Check the gauge or the flow from the lance. If pressure is still present, release it only by the manufacturer's method and only if the worker is trained and authorised to do so. If the method is unclear or the worker is not authorised, call the supervisor and wait. Tell the supervisor what happened, record it as a near miss, and note the step that was not followed.

workedExamples.situation: At the end of a job, a hose shows a bulge close to one fitting. The worker thinks the bulge is small and that the hose will last one more job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the hose be used again, and what must the worker record?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A bulge is one of the defects the Safe Work Australia guide lists for a hose assembly. Tag the hose as defective, move it away from the working equipment and do not use it. Do not cut out the bulge and rejoin the hose. Record the item, the date, the defect and the finder on the defect log, and photograph the defect with permission if the site allows it. Report the hose to the supervisor, who arranges repair or replacement through an authorised route. The hose returns to service only after it passes a recorded test.

workedExamples.situation: A chemical container has a worn label and a cracked lid. The worker wants to pour the contents into a plain spray bottle for the next morning.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should happen to the chemical, and what must be checked first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not decant the chemical into an unlabelled container. Keep the container closed, move it to the designated storage point and report the cracked lid to the supervisor. Find the product name and the safety data sheet from the remaining label or the supplier record before anyone uses or stores it again. Follow the business's handling and waste procedure for the damaged container. If the product cannot be identified, treat it as unidentified and do not use it.

equipmentAndPpe: The manufacturer's manual for the specific machine, with the shutdown sequence and the release method.
Defect tags, a quarantine location and a defect log.
Eye protection. The Safe Work Australia guide calls for eye protection anywhere close to jetting work, and a face shield for the person controlling the flow, to a standard it names.

Waterproof clothing and safety footwear. The guide points to the AS 3765 series for waterproof clothing and AS/NZS 2210.3 for safety footwear, for industrial jetting. For smaller machines, the risk assessment sets the PPE.
Gloves to the risk assessment, using the AS/NZS 2161 series named in the guide where the assessment requires them.
Hearing protection where noise cannot be eliminated.
Labelled chemical containers, closed storage and the safety data sheets for each product.
Drip tray and waste container for used chemical and wash water, as the site rules direct.
Camera or phone for defect photographs, used only with the owner's or site's permission.

commonErrors.error: Disconnecting a hose or lance while the machine still holds pressure.
commonErrors.prevention: Isolate the supply, release the pressure by the manufacturer's method and confirm the safe state before any disconnection.

commonErrors.error: Dragging hoses across concrete, glass, paint or stone during collection.
commonErrors.prevention: Lift and coil the hose, and keep it clear of delicate surfaces and sharp edges.

commonErrors.error: Using a suspected defective hose for one more job.
commonErrors.prevention: Tag the hose as defective, move it away from the working equipment, log it and report it.

commonErrors.error: Repairing a fitting with a spare from another machine, or cutting and rejoining a hose.
commonErrors.prevention: Report the defect. Only an authorised person repairs equipment, using an approved part, and the hose returns to service only after a recorded test.

commonErrors.error: Moving a chemical into an unlabelled bottle.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the original label. If the label is lost, identify the product from the supplier record and its safety data sheet before using it.

commonErrors.error: Doing a quick visual check at the end of the day and skipping the record.
commonErrors.prevention: Complete the inspection and the shutdown checklist every time, and record defects even when the item is still working.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on a roof, from an elevated work platform or on a solar system, and completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. In New South Wales, a boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where its boom length is 11 metres or more, so a shorter boom may not need it in that state (SafeWork NSW, High risk work licences, last modified 15 June 2026 per page metadata). Western Australia, where the WP licence covers a boom length of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe WA, last updated 13 August 2026); Tasmania, where the WP class covers booms of 11 metres or more (WorkSafe Tasmania, check the classes, last updated 1 December 2023); and the Northern Territory, where the licence class covers a boom length of 11 metres or more (NT WorkSafe bulletin, no date shown). In Queensland, the WorkSafe QLD page, search snippet, date not shown, says that elevated work platforms less than 11 metres in length are not included in the boom-type definition. Whether a boom-length threshold applies in Victoria is not confirmed by an official source. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code measures the boom from the original design, and it requires no licence for shorter booms, but it still expects the operator to be trained. Scissor lifts need no WP licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory, where the operator's competence must still be assessed. Check the rule for the state or territory of the work and obtain written employer authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule: stop at once, make the area safe and tell your supervisor before work restarts if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; if wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; if you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or a live part; if a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; if the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or if you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation the work requires.

Electrical notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In New South Wales, electrical wiring work covers repairing and changing an installation, and the licensing page leaves out electrical articles connected to an outlet. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

Equipment currency: the Safe Work Australia jetting guide is dated December 2013 and has no stated edition number. Its content on inspection, isolation and PPE is used here as a national reference. Confirm it against the current edition and the manufacturer's data before relying on it for a particular machine.

qualityStandard: The cleaning area is secured and the manufacturer's shutdown sequence is followed in order.
Pressure is released by an authorised method, and the equipment is confirmed safe before any disconnection.
Every hose, fitting and connection is inspected, and each defect is tagged, logged and reported.
Hoses are collected without dragging across delicate surfaces, and chemicals are stored in labelled containers with their safety data sheets available.
Nothing is repaired without authority, and every defect or maintenance request is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Completed shutdown checklist for each job, signed by the worker and checked by the supervisor
Defect log with the item, date, defect, finder and tag status for each quarantined item
Maintenance request raised for each defect, with its outcome
Chemical storage record showing the product, its container and the safety data sheet reference
Near-miss or incident record for any disconnection under pressure or any unsafe shutdown
summary: A safe finish includes a controlled shutdown, pressure release, isolation and the prevention of residual chemical or wash-water exposure.
The machine can hold energy after it is switched off, so the manufacturer's sequence is followed in order and the safe state is confirmed before disconnection.
Hoses and fittings are inspected at each use and at shutdown. Defective items are tagged out, logged and reported, and they return to service only after a recorded test.
Repairs need authority. Completing this lesson gives no licence or permission for regulated work.

knowledgeChecks.question: What must be confirmed before a hose is disconnected at the end of a job?
options: The hose has been dragged across the surface so it coils quickly and neatly for the van
The machine is switched off at the hose while it still holds pressure in the line and the wand
Pressure has been released by the manufacturer's method and the machine is confirmed safe
A spare fitting from another machine is ready to replace the coupling on the hose and the wand

knowledgeChecks.question: A hose shows a bulge close to a fitting at the end of a job. What is the correct response?
options: Wrap the bulge with tape and use the hose on a low-pressure job for the rest of the day
Cut out the bulge and rejoin the hose before the next job starts on the same day
Use the hose once more, because a small bulge is not a defect in use and it is fine
Tag the hose as defective, log it, move it away from working equipment and report it

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaning chemical has a worn label and no safety data sheet is on hand. What should happen?
options: Pour it into a plain spray bottle so it is ready for the morning shift and the whole crew to use
Use it, because the colour of the liquid shows what it is and how strong it is for the job
Keep it closed, do not use it, and identify the product from its supplier record and safety data sheet first
Ask the client which product is safest to use on the surface and on the whole job at the site
